I wasn't officially diagnosed (what WAS called) Asperger's until 2 years ago (I'm 35 now), but my parents knew a long time ago. I understand a lot of what you're going through. Hell, I trapped myself in an abusive marriage for nearly 10 years because I was worried no one else would have me and I tried to learn from all my mistakes. Eventually, she nearly managed to talk me into killing myself so I've got a lot of emotional scars. I'm still healing, but I've made a lot of progress.

One thing you have to be ready for is the depression. Since generic daily affirmations don't work for me, I'd realized I have to honestly observe myself and consider my positive attributes. It wasn't easy, but I managed to make a list and put it on my bathroom mirror to see every day. If I'm overwhelmed or depression is hitting too hard, it helps to look at it and distract myself from subjective negativity with honest positivity.

I also recognize where a lot of my own problems lie, so I consider what I can fix and what I can't. For things I can fix, I work on developing habits. For things I can't fix, I try to find ways to function around it. For example, I have terrible memory and a lot of trouble focusing, so I carry a pen and a small pad of paper to notate important things and schedule as much as I can in my Google Calendar so I have automatic reminders.

For social interactions, here are few tricks I learned:

  • If you have trouble with eye contact, talk with you're hand. I don't mean ASL (though ASL would be useful if you're none verbal). Imagine someone telling a fish story and they're acting out what they're saying. Looking at the imaginary objects you're pantomiming gives you a reason not to make eye contact.

  • If you're like me and over analyze things, getting out of you're own head is important. Sometimes, you have to tell yourself to "shut up and do it" to get anything done. It's how you meet new people and try new things. You have to learn how to muffle the "what if" voice in your head to get anything done. It'll help reduce anxiety and let you relax and enjoy yourself.

  • Some ASD discussion groups might help. Unfortunately, these groups tend to become political every time. All the ASD groups I was a part of were slowly taken over by leftists and trans people, but it can still be good to hear from people experiencing similar things as yourself and learn how they deal with certain situations.

Not sure if it helped, but I wish you luck. Just remember, things aren't usually as bad as we tend to think they are.

Serious advice: join an improv group. It's the art of playing along, which is what we do socially. Remember in conversation FORD: Family, Occupation, Recreation, Dreams. Learn to listen and ask interesting questions.

If you play along, take interest, and intrigue people, you'll be on your way to being better socially than 90% of people.

The rules don't come naturally to you so learn them and play along. Body language dictionaries are your friends. Figure it out and manipulate it to your advantage. Armed with that knowledge put yourself in situations that push you outside of your comfort zone and boundaries, experience grants courage.
Let go of your past, concentrate on the present and future, you can't change what's already happened.
